Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and let $\F$ be a codimension one, $C^\infty$ foliation on $M$, with isolated singularities of Morse type. The study and classification of pairs $(M,\F)$ is a challenging (and difficult) problem. In this setting, a classical result due to Reeb \cite{Reeb} states that a manifold admitting a foliation with exactly two center-type singularities is a sphere. In particular this is true if the foliation is given by a function. Along these lines a result due to Eells and Kuiper \cite{Ku-Ee} classify manifolds having a real-valued function admitting exactly three non-degenerate singular points. In the present paper, we prove a generalization of the above mentioned results. To do this, we first describe the possible arrangements of pairs of singularities and the corresponding codimension one invariant sets, and then we give an elimination procedure for suitable center-saddle and some saddle-saddle configurations (of consecutive indices). In the second part, we investigate if other classical results, such as Haefliger and Novikov (Compact Leaf) theorems, proved for regular foliations, still hold true in presence of singularities. At this purpose, in the singular set, $Sing(\F)$ of the foliation $\F$, we consider {\em{weakly stable}} components, that we define as those components admitting a neighborhood where all leaves are compact. If $Sing(\F)$ admits only weakly stable components, given by smoothly embedded curves diffeomorphic to $S^1$, we are able to extend Haefliger's theorem. Finally, the existence of a closed curve, transverse to the foliation, leads us to state a Novikov-type result.

Let \(M\) be a smooth manifold, and let \(\F\) be a codimension-one \(C^\infty\) foliation on \(M\) with isolated singularities of Morse type. The study and classification of pairs \((M,\F)\) constitute a challenging problem. In this setting, a classical result of Reeb \cite{Reeb} states that a manifold admitting a foliation with exactly two center-type singularities is a sphere. In particular, this conclusion holds when the foliation is defined by a function. Along these lines, a result of Eells and Kuiper \cite{Ku-Ee} classifies manifolds admitting a real-valued function with exactly three nondegenerate singular points.

In the present paper, we establish a generalization of the aforementioned results. To this end, we first describe the possible configurations of pairs of singularities and the corresponding codimension-one invariant sets. We then provide an elimination procedure for suitable center-saddle configurations and certain saddle-saddle configurations with consecutive indices.

In the second part, we investigate whether other classical results—such as the Haefliger and Novikov compact leaf theorems, originally proved for regular foliations—continue to hold in the presence of singularities. To this end, within the singular set \(Sing(\F)\) of the foliation \(\F\), we consider \emph{weakly stable} components, defined as those admitting a neighborhood in which every leaf is compact. If \(Sing(\F)\) consists solely of weakly stable components given by smoothly embedded curves diffeomorphic to \(S^1\), we are able to extend Haefliger’s theorem. Finally, the existence of a closed curve transverse to the foliation allows us to formulate a Novikov-type result.

Let \(M\) be a smooth manifold equipped with a \(C^\infty\), codimension-one foliation \(\F\) whose singularities are isolated and of Morse type. Understanding and classifying such pairs \((M,\F)\) is a difficult problem. A classical theorem of Reeb \cite{Reeb} asserts that any manifold carrying a foliation with precisely two center-type singularities must be a sphere; in particular, the conclusion applies when the foliation is induced by a function. In a related direction, Eells and Kuiper \cite{Ku-Ee} classified manifolds that admit a real-valued function with exactly three nondegenerate critical points.

This paper extends these results. We begin by determining the possible configurations formed by pairs of singularities together with their associated invariant sets of codimension one. We then develop a method for eliminating appropriate center–saddle configurations, as well as certain saddle–saddle configurations whose indices are consecutive.

The second part examines whether classical theorems for nonsingular foliations—specifically the compact-leaf results of Haefliger and Novikov—remain valid when singularities are allowed. For this purpose, a component of the singular set \(Sing(\F)\) is called \emph{weakly stable} if it has a neighborhood in which every leaf is compact. We obtain an extension of Haefliger’s theorem when all components of \(Sing(\F)\) are weakly stable and are smoothly embedded curves diffeomorphic to \(S^1\). Finally, the presence of a closed curve transverse to the foliation yields a Novikov-type theorem.

The paper investigates the classification of codimension-one smooth foliations with isolated singularities of Morse type on smooth manifolds. Its results broaden two classical lines of research: Reeb’s theorem concerning foliations with two center-type singularities, and the Eells–Kuiper classification of manifolds that admit smooth functions with exactly three nondegenerate critical points.

A central part of the analysis concerns the possible configurations formed by pairs of singularities and the codimension-one invariant sets associated with them. The authors identify the relevant geometric and dynamical arrangements and study how these local configurations influence the global structure of the foliation.

The paper also develops procedures for simplifying the singular foliation by eliminating appropriate pairs of singularities. In particular, it treats certain center–saddle configurations, as well as saddle–saddle pairs whose Morse indices are consecutive. These elimination techniques provide an important tool for reducing complicated foliations to simpler models and thereby advancing their classification.

Finally, the authors extend Haefliger’s theorem to a setting in which the singular set is no longer discrete but consists of weakly stable embedded circles. They also establish a Novikov-type result showing that the existence of a closed transverse curve imposes strong global restrictions on the foliation. Together, these results connect local Morse-theoretic data with the global topology and dynamics of singular codimension-one foliations.

This paper extends several classical classification and existence results for codimension-one smooth foliations to foliations with isolated Morse-type singularities. The central objective is to understand how the topology of the ambient manifold, the dynamics of the regular leaves, and the local behavior near singular points interact. Particular attention is given to pairs of singularities and to invariant subsets associated with their stable and unstable separatrices.

A principal part of the analysis concerns elimination procedures for singularity pairs. For a center-saddle pair satisfying suitable geometric and dynamical conditions, the foliation can be modified locally so that both singularities disappear without changing it outside a prescribed neighborhood. A corresponding procedure is developed for pairs of saddle singularities whose Morse indices are consecutive. These cancellation results provide a mechanism for simplifying singular foliations and reducing their study to configurations with fewer critical points. The role of separatrix connections, invariant regions, and possible obstructions to cancellation is examined throughout.

The paper also investigates how classical compact-leaf theorems behave in the presence of singularities. Results traditionally formulated for nonsingular codimension-one foliations are reconsidered in a setting where the singular locus may have positive dimension. In particular, an extension of Haefliger’s theorem is established when the singular set consists of embedded circles satisfying a weak stability condition. Under appropriate hypotheses, the topology and holonomy near these singular circles still force the existence of compact invariant leaves or analogous compact structures.

Finally, the existence of a closed curve transverse to the foliation is used to obtain a Novikov-type conclusion. The transverse curve imposes global restrictions on the leaf structure and leads, under the stated assumptions, to the existence of a compact leaf or a related Reeb-type phenomenon. Together, these results show that essential features of classical foliation theory survive in singular settings once the local models, invariant sets, and cancellation mechanisms are treated carefully. The work therefore broadens foundational classification and compactness theorems from regular codimension-one foliations to a substantial class of singular foliations.
outputs.L5:
**The Last Signal**

The lighthouse had been dark for years, but every night, Elias climbed its spiral stairs and listened to the radio.

“Let the silence speak,” his father had once told him.

Then, during a winter storm, a faint Morse signal broke through the static:

**... --- ...**

The message repeated until dawn.

Elias switched on the lighthouse lamp. Far beyond the cliffs, a lost ship answered with three flashes of light.

For the first time in years, the tower had a purpose again.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a mathematics paper on codimension-one smooth foliations with isolated Morse-type singularities, generalizing results of Reeb and Eells–Kuiper and extending Haefliger and Novikov theorems to the singular setting.
counterfactuals.output: We study codimension-one smooth foliations on closed manifolds whose singular set consists of isolated Morse-type singularities. Under natural hypotheses on transversality, holonomy, and the configuration of centers and saddles, we establish global structure and classification results extending classical theorems for nonsingular foliations. In particular, we prove singular analogues of the Haefliger and Novikov compact-leaf theorems, showing that suitable null-homotopic transverse loops or vanishing-cycle phenomena force the existence of compact leaves and Reeb-type components. We also analyze the topology of the leaf space and the way regular leaves attach across singular levels. As applications, we obtain rigidity theorems generalizing Reeb’s sphere theorem and the Eells–Kuiper characterization: foliations with minimal Morse singular data force the ambient manifold to be a sphere or, in the exceptional cases, an Eells–Kuiper manifold. These results provide a unified framework relating Morse theory, holonomy, and the global topology of singular foliations.

Let $M$ be a closed smooth manifold and let $\mathcal{F}$ be a
codimension-one $C^\infty$ foliation on $M$ whose singular set consists

the pairs $(M,\mathcal{F})$ in terms of the topology of $M$, the indices

procedure: under suitable compatibility conditions, pairs of

constrains the possible global configurations. Finally, we prove a
Novikov-type theorem asserting that appropriate vanishing-cycle or
fundamental-group conditions force the occurrence of a compact leaf
and, in the relevant cases, a Reeb-type component. These results yield

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a paper that studies center–saddle and saddle–saddle configurations in singular foliations, develops elimination procedures for consecutive-index singularities, and investigates analogues of the Haefliger and Novikov compact-leaf results.
counterfactuals.output:
The paper develops a Morse-theoretic approach to codimension-one singular foliations, focusing on foliations whose isolated singularities are centers or saddles.

Its first part analyzes how singularities can be connected by leaves and separatrices. Two configurations are central:

- **Center–saddle configurations**, where a saddle lies on the boundary of the region of compact leaves surrounding a center.
- **Saddle–saddle configurations**, where separatrices of distinct saddles interact, producing connections that may obstruct simplification of the foliation.

Using local Morse models and surgery on saturated neighborhoods, the authors establish **elimination or cancellation procedures for singularities of consecutive Morse index**. Under suitable compatibility and absence-of-obstruction conditions, a center–saddle pair—or more generally an appropriate pair of consecutive-index singularities—can be removed while preserving the foliation outside a controlled region. Saddle connections are identified as the principal exceptional cases.

The paper then applies these techniques to singular versions of classical compact-leaf theorems. It investigates analogues of:

- **Haefliger’s theorem**, which forces compact leaves under topological restrictions on the ambient manifold; and
- **Novikov’s compact-leaf theorem**, which links global topology, transverse behavior, and the existence of compact leaves or Reeb-type components.

The main message is that much of the classical theory survives for Morse singular foliations after singular configurations are classified and cancellable pairs are eliminated. However, center–saddle basins and saddle–saddle separatrix connections introduce genuinely new phenomena, so the singular analogues require additional hypotheses. Overall, the paper combines local singularity theory, Morse cancellation, and global foliation topology to reduce complicated singular foliations to simpler models in which compact-leaf results can be recovered.

counterfactuals.output: We study Morse foliations on closed smooth manifolds, viewed as codimension-one singular foliations whose isolated singularities are locally modeled by nondegenerate critical points. Taking Reeb’s two-center sphere theorem as the basic rigidity paradigm, we examine how the topology of the ambient manifold is constrained by the number, indices, and mutual position of the singularities. The three-critical-point case is discussed in relation to the Eells–Kuiper classification and its projective-plane-type manifolds. Our main framework associates invariant saturated sets with distinguished pairs of singularities, providing a geometric means of detecting cancellation, separation, and global decomposition phenomena. We also introduce weakly stable singular circles and analyze their role as limiting configurations for nearby leaves and as organizing structures for the foliation’s singular dynamics. These ideas yield a unified perspective on Reeb-type stability, singularity pairing, and classification questions for Morse foliations with few singular components.

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a concise academic overview of new results on codimension-one foliations with isolated Morse-type singularities, explaining how classical classification and compact-leaf theorems are generalized when the singular set consists of smoothly embedded circles?
counterfactuals.output:
Recent work replaces isolated Morse critical points by **Bott–Morse singularities**. For a codimension-one foliation \(\mathcal F\) on an \(n\)-manifold \(M\), the singular locus is a finite union of embedded circles \(C_i\), and near each \(C_i\) there are coordinates in which \(\mathcal F\) is defined by the level sets of a nondegenerate quadratic form on the normal \((n-1)\)-disk. Thus each circle has a transverse Morse index and is of center or saddle type. The normal bundle and its monodromy provide new invariants absent in the point-singularity case.

Under the usual orientability and stability assumptions, the classical Reeb-type classification extends as follows. If every singular circle is of center type, a connected closed manifold has two singular components and decomposes as  
\[
M \cong D(\nu C_-)\cup_{\varphi}D(\nu C_+),
\]
where \(D(\nu C_\pm)\) are the normal disk bundles of the two circles and \(\varphi\) identifies their sphere-bundle boundaries. Every regular leaf is compact and is diffeomorphic to the corresponding \(S^{n-2}\)-bundle over \(S^1\); when the normal bundles are trivial, it is \(S^1\times S^{n-2}\). This generalizes the classical statement that a Morse foliation with only center singularities is obtained by gluing two disks and hence, in the simplest case, lives on a sphere.

Reeb global stability and compact-leaf theorems likewise admit a Bott–Morse version. A compact regular leaf with finite holonomy—often ensured by finite fundamental group—has a saturated stable neighborhood, and compactness propagates through the foliation until a singular circle is reached. With only centers, all regular leaves are compact and the leaf space is an interval whose endpoints represent the singular circles. When saddle circles are allowed, the leaf space becomes a finite graph: edges correspond to families of compact regular leaves and vertices encode center or saddle components. Additional hypotheses excluding saddle connections or nontrivial holonomy are then necessary, since these phenomena can obstruct global compactness.

Thus the point-singularity theory survives in a fibered form: singular points are replaced by critical circles, disks by normal disk bundles, spheres by sphere bundles over \(S^1\), and the interval-like leaf space by a graph carrying the topology and monodromy of the singular set.
